distractors.option: Last summer we drove North for two days to visit my cousins, who live in the Midwest.
distractors.reason: Capitalizing compass directions used as directions is one of the most common grade 5 errors.

distractors.option: Last summer we drove North for two days to visit my cousins, who live in the midwest.
distractors.reason: Students who have the rule backwards (direction capped, region not) pick this.

distractors.option: Last summer we drove north for two days to visit my cousins, who live in the midwest.
distractors.reason: Lowercasing region names like midwest is very common; students treat it like the plain direction.

distractors.option: On Saturday, my Uncle and grandma drove us to the county fair.
distractors.reason: Students mix up which family word gets capitalized and often get it exactly backwards.

distractors.option: On Saturday, my Uncle and Grandma drove us to the county fair.
distractors.reason: Capitalizing every family title, even after 'my', is a very frequent error.

distractors.option: On Saturday, my uncle and grandma drove us to the county fair.
distractors.reason: Students who learned 'don't capitalize family words' apply it to Grandma used as a name too.

distractors.option: Because Hana signed up for french this year, her science class moved to the last period of the day.
distractors.reason: Students treat all school subjects alike and lowercase languages too.

distractors.option: Because Hana signed up for French this year, her Science class moved to the last period of the day.
distractors.reason: Capitalizing all school subjects is a very common habit from schedules and folders.

distractors.option: Because Hana signed up for french this year, her Science class moved to the last period of the day.
distractors.reason: Weak students are inconsistent with subject names; reversing the rule is a real pattern.

distractors.option: Our class report compares the civil war with other wars fought during the nineteenth century.
distractors.reason: Many students do not recognize named historical events as proper nouns.

distractors.option: Our class report compares the civil war with other wars fought during the Nineteenth Century.
distractors.reason: Less likely than the others, but weak students capitalize inconsistently and 'Nineteenth Century' looks official to them.

distractors.option: Our class report compares the Civil War with other wars fought during the Nineteenth Century.
distractors.reason: Capitalizing centuries alongside named eras is a very common overgeneralization.

Dropping the double s is one of the most frequent spellings I see.
Swapping which letter doubles is the textbook 'necessary' error.

Adding a d by analogy with 'knowledge' or 'ledge' is very common.
Combines both common errors; frequently seen in student writing.
Single r is probably the single most common misspelling of this word.
-ance vs -ence confusion is common; the doubles look right.

distractors.option: When the storm ended we swept the porch, picked up fallen branches, and dragged the trash cans back to the curb.
distractors.reason: Leaving out the comma after an introductory clause is extremely common.

distractors.option: When the storm ended, we swept the porch picked up fallen branches and dragged the trash cans back to the curb.
distractors.reason: Students often leave out commas in a series of verb phrases.

distractors.option: When the storm ended we swept the porch picked up fallen branches and dragged the trash cans back to the curb.
distractors.reason: Weak writers often use no commas at all; a quick reader may not see that anything is missing.

distractors.option: Our school library which reopened last month after the flood, now stays open until five o'clock.
distractors.reason: Putting only the closing comma (a pause before the verb) is a common error.

distractors.option: Our school library, which reopened last month after the flood now stays open until five o'clock.
distractors.reason: Forgetting the closing comma of the pair is the most common nonessential-clause error.

distractors.option: Our school library which reopened last month after the flood now stays open until five o'clock.
distractors.reason: Many students don't set off the clause at all, and it reads smoothly to them.

distractors.option: After a long boring bus ride, Mia pulled on her new winter coat and stepped into the snow.
distractors.reason: Leaving the comma out between coordinate adjectives is very common.

distractors.option: After a long boring bus ride, Mia pulled on her new, winter coat and stepped into the snow.
distractors.reason: Students who half-know the rule put the comma between the wrong pair.

distractors.option: After a long, boring bus ride, Mia pulled on her new, winter coat and stepped into the snow.
distractors.reason: Putting a comma between every pair of adjectives is the classic overgeneralization.

distractors.option: Dripping with melted cheese, Marco carried the pizza to the table.
distractors.reason: The classic dangling modifier sounds natural to students; many pick it.

distractors.option: Marco, dripping with melted cheese, carried the pizza to the table.
distractors.reason: Plainly says Marco is dripping cheese; even weak students see the joke.

distractors.option: Marco carried the pizza to the table, dripping with melted cheese.
distractors.reason: Putting the modifier at the end feels natural and most students wouldn't notice it now points to the table.
